analysis.one_liner: Lets individuals and businesses switch to a flat tax and repeals estate and gift taxes.
analysis.headline: The Flat Tax Act, which would have let people and businesses opt into a flat 17% tax and repealed the estate tax, died in committee with zero cosponsors and never came up for a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created an optional flat tax system: any individual or business could irrevocably choose to pay 19% for two years, then 17% forever after, in place of the normal income tax. For individuals, only cash wages, retirement withdrawals, and unemployment benefits would count as income, with a large standard deduction and no credits. For businesses, profits would be taxed at the same flat rate after subtracting purchases, wages, and retirement contributions. Separately, it would repeal the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely, and would require a two-thirds vote of both chambers to ever raise the flat rate or shrink the deductions.
analysis.who_benefits: The biggest winners are high-income households and business owners. Someone who elects the flat tax pays nothing on capital gains, dividends, interest, or rental income — the flat tax base includes only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, not investment income [S3]. Businesses would pay 17% on profits instead of the current 21% corporate rate, on a base with generous deductions for purchases and wages [S3]. Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes would directly benefit the wealthiest estates, which are the only ones large enough to owe those taxes [S2][S3]. Some working families would also pay less, because the standard deduction is large and the rate is low.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, business owners, and wealthy estates

how_it_helps.text: Individuals electing the flat tax would pay 19% for two years and 17% after that, only on cash wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, minus a standard deduction that starts around $16,248 for singles and $32,496 for joint filers, adjusted for inflation [S2][S3].

Businesses electing the flat tax would pay the same flat rate on profits after deducting the cost of business inputs, cash wages, and retirement contributions, replacing the current corporate income tax and alternative minimum tax [S2][S3].
The bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and gifts after 2022, eliminating federal tax on large inheritances [S2][S3].

The bill would make it much harder to raise these taxes later: any bill increasing the flat rate or reducing the standard or business deductions would need a two-thirds vote of the House and Senate rather than a simple majority [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on the federal treasury and, ultimately, on everyone who does not elect the flat tax. Because the flat tax base excludes investment income entirely and repeals the estate tax, moving even a slice of high-income taxpayers and businesses into it cuts federal revenue, which means larger deficits or future cuts to programs and services that everyone relies on [S3]. Ordinary workers who elect the flat tax would also lose every tax credit they currently qualify for, such as the child tax credit and earned income tax credit [S3]. Additionally, tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local government employers electing the system would owe a new tax on the value of employee benefits like health insurance [S3].

drawbacks.text: The flat tax base counts only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, so a person electing it would owe nothing on capital gains, dividends, interest, or rents — a structural benefit concentrated among the highest earners [S3].

Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes removes the only federal tax on very large inheritances, a change whose benefits go almost entirely to the wealthiest families [S2][S3].
Anyone electing the flat tax loses all tax credits, including the child tax credit and earned income tax credit that low- and middle-income families rely on [S3].
The two-thirds vote requirement would lock in the low rate and large deductions, making it far harder for a future Congress to raise revenue through this system even if needs change [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some working families genuinely would owe less: a large standard deduction plus a 17% rate means many moderate-wage earners would see their bill drop, and the system would be simpler for those who elect it. But the design gives its largest benefits to people with the most investment income and the largest estates, who would owe nothing at all on gains, dividends, or inheritances under the election, and the revenue given up would have to be replaced through deficits, spending cuts, or higher taxes on everyone else. The bill was also lightly built — it was introduced with no cosponsors and never received a committee analysis or scoring, so its revenue effects were never officially examined [S4][S5].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means and Rules committees in February 2023, neither committee ever took it up, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without a single cosponsor, hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the Flat Tax Act on February 14, 2023 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Rules Committee, the committees that handle tax legislation and floor procedures [S1][S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor during the entire two-year Congress [S4].
The committees never scheduled a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the House floor, and it expired with the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the existing tax code — including the estate tax, the current corporate rate, and credits like the child tax credit — remained in place, so ordinary taxpayers kept the status quo while high earners and large estates did not receive the new exemptions. The bill's sponsor and the idea's supporters lost nothing except the bill itself, and no constituency gained materially from its death other than the preservation of current law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing tax code stayed in place

for.name: Rep. Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Flat Tax Act in the House; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction over tax legislation (Chair Jason Smith, R)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 14, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so no party breakdown exists; its only support was a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party [S4][S5].

industries.note: The flat tax base excludes capital gains, dividends, interest, and rents entirely [S3], and the bill repeals the estate and gift taxes [S2][S3], so the wealthiest households would owe dramatically less while the lost revenue falls on the budget everyone shares. Their gain would come at the public's cost.

Businesses electing the flat tax would pay 17% on profits — down from the 21% corporate rate — on a base with deductions for purchases, wages, and retirement contributions [S2][S3]. The revenue reduction would be borne by the treasury and non-electing taxpayers.

Employers that elect the flat tax and are tax-exempt or government agencies would owe a new 17–19% tax on the value of noncash employee benefits like health coverage [S3], raising their cost of providing benefits to workers.

A simpler optional tax with a large standard deduction and no credits would mean less compliance work for electing taxpayers [S2], though because the election is optional the industry would not be eliminated.
